headline: ICE didn’t know 5-year-old boy was in car when officer fired, Mullin says
author: Tim Craig, David Nakamura, Silvia Foster-Frau, Ted Hesson

paragraphs.text: NEW YORK — Federal authorities on Friday strongly denounced the reaction of New York officials to the shooting of a Dominican man by a U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement officer, casting the man as the aggressor who used his car to ram two government vehicles and accelerate toward officers despite having a 5-year-old in the back seat.

Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said the ICE officers did not know the boy was in the vehicle driven by Oscar Belgal, 28, who was struck in the neck during the shooting Thursday afternoon in New York City. Belgal was treated at the scene and taken to a hospital before being moved to a detention facility outside the state, authorities said.
Mullin said Belgal, the boy’s father, would face criminal prosecution and be placed in deportation proceedings.

“He knew he had a child in the car and chose to accelerate at a high-rate of speed,” Mullin said at a news conference in Washington, flanked by senior ICE officials. “He’s a criminal, a thug, a gang banger. The outrage should be with him endangering a 5-year-old.”

New York officials, including Gov. Kathy Hochul (D) and New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani (D), have denounced the agency and demanded that ICE pause enforcement operations in the state. Mamdani called on federal officials to “abolish ICE.”
“No, we’re not putting a pause on enforcement,” Mullin said. “I’m sorry, we’re not. In fact, I’m not sorry.”
Mullin accused New York officials of failing to cooperate with immigration enforcement efforts to take custody of undocumented immigrants who are arrested for state and local offenses.

New York City has policies that limit local law enforcement from sharing certain information with federal officers or honoring detainer requests unless immigrants have been convicted of violent crimes. The state also has policies to prevent federal authorities from accessing motor vehicle and drivers’ license records of immigrants without a court order or search warrant.

Mullin said ICE had issued 14,766 detainers in New York since President Donald Trump took office last year to take custody of people in New York jails. But, he said, the state has failed to cooperate. “Silence is what we got from the state of New York,” he said.

Mullin said he spoke with Mamdani on Thursday night and the mayor asked him to release Belgal, prompting Trump to tell Mamdani that the administration would transfer custody to local police if they are willing to pursue criminal charges against Belgal.
“The mayor said, ‘We are not detaining him,’” Mullin said.
Mamdani did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

ICE and the Department of Homeland Security have faced widespread public outrage over aggressive enforcement tactics. Earlier this year, federal officers fatally shot two U.S. citizens during a surge in operations in Minneapolis in January. Since July, two immigrants have been shot and killed by ICE officers who fired into their vehicles.
Democrats, immigration advocates and family members of the deceased say that ICE is using excessive force against people who do not represent a threat.

Mullin, a former U.S. senator from Oklahoma, took over DHS in late April, promising to take a quieter approach than his predecessor, Kristi L. Noem. The agency has backed off from conducting large-scale raids that previously led to broad community protests and a drop in support for the president’s deportation agenda. Still, under Mullin’s watch, ICE has significantly increased detentions, arresting over 50,000 immigrants in August, which DHS said was a record.

Trump officials have consistently stated that their goal is to keep Americans safe by targeting enforcement against “the worst of the worst” — undocumented immigrants who have committed violent crimes or repeated offenses. But arrest data shows that many of those being arrested have only civil immigration violations. More than half of all the people ICE arrested in July did not have a criminal record, according to a Post analysis.

New York Police Commissioner Jessica Tisch and Mamdani told reporters late Thursday that the ICE officers were not wearing clothing that indicated they were law enforcement personnel and said at least one officer was carrying a long gun.

“They wore construction vests and masks that concealed their faces. There was no reasonable way to identify them as ICE agents,” Mamdani said. “School had just gotten out. The street was crowded with families and children.”

Mullin said the officers were conducting a standard undercover operation against Belgal, who officers had unsuccessfully attempted to arrest in September before he fled. Belgal has lived in the United States for three years and been accused of crimes including grand larceny, robbery and theft armed with a dangerous weapon, authorities said.

ICE officers “identified themselves and gave lawful orders when they approached the vehicle,” Mullin said. “Not to mention he knew he was wanted. He had fled once ... I know he knew his day was coming.”
Mullin said authorities believe Belgal is connected to a gang that was involved in the shooting of a U.S. Customs and Border Protection officer last year.
“It’s shameful we’re giving this case so much attention when this was a thug — the worst of the worst,” Mullin said of Belgal.

Rep. Adriano Espaillat (D-New York) said he visited with Belgal’s 5-year-old son and his mother last night. He said the family told him Belgal picked up his son from school, put him in a car seat in the back and then went to visit family members in the area when he was shot.
The child is physically unharmed, but Espaillat said the family told him he is “traumatized by this whole experience.”

The lawmaker said he was not aware of Belgal’s alleged criminal history, but that regardless, the decision to fire at his vehicle in the middle of the day in a residential area put many people at risk.
“Any neighborhood in the country will be appalled of this kind of stuff happening right in the middle of it,” Espaillat said. “If anything, they were the ones that put our community in danger.”
